transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-12
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 46 minutes (scheduled 45)
Attendees: Grace Li (Redwood AE), Marcus O'Neill (Redwood SE), Elena Park (Novus - Head of ML), Ravi Singh (Novus - Platform), Marta Lopez (Novus - CTO)

Summary:
Short discovery focused on integration options for Redwood's hosted/dedicated/private offerings. Main topics: SDK support (Python/Node), LangChain & LlamaIndex integrations, gateway/proxy patterns for routing, rate limits & quotas, observability hooks and what telemetry is available for per-route token cost and latency. Follow-ups: pricing deck, benchmark plan, traffic profile.

Transcript:
[00:00] Grace Li: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Grace from Redwood, and with me is Marcus, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Elena Park: Hi Grace, hi Marcus. All good, thanks. We wanted to kick off integration discovery — figure out how quickly we can prototype on your hosted API and what it looks like to move to dedicated or private later.
[00:12] Marcus O'Neill: Great. Quick agenda: SDKs and prebuilt integrations, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy patterns (we've seen folks put a sidecar or central gateway), rate limiting/quotas, and observability hooks. Then we'll capture next steps. Does that work?
[00:20] Marta Lopez: Yes perfect. We're especially worried about latency and cost — and also security for customer data.
[00:25] Ravi Singh: Also curious about per-route tracing and being able to attribute costs back to product teams.
[00:28] Marcus O'Neill: Totally — Redwood Console has per-route token breakdowns and tracing hooks. You can attach route metadata so you can break down token spend by team or feature. There's an API to pull that data too for internal chargeback.
[00:37] Elena Park: Is that available on hosted or only dedicated/private?
[00:40] Grace Li: Per-route observability is available on Hosted and Dedicated; for Private (VPC/on-prem) you get the same telemetry but delivery depends on your network setup — we can stream audit logs to your logging endpoint or you can pull via the control plane with customer-managed retention.
[00:51] Ravi Singh: When you say stream logs, are we talking syslog, S3, or something else? Our security team prefers S3 + KMS encryption.
[00:56] Marcus O'Neill: S3 is supported. We also offer KMS integrations (bring-your-own keys) and can integrate with HSMs for private infra. For on-prem, there are connectors to forward logs to internal SIEM.
[01:05] Elena Park: Nice. On the SDK front — we primarily use Python backend and Node for some edge services. Do you have official SDKs and LangChain connectors?
[01:12] Grace Li: Yes, official SDKs for Python and Node. We maintain LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters; they're first-class integrations. Marcus, do you want to cover the connector details?
[01:18] Marcus O'Neill: Sure — the LangChain connector works with the standard LLM interface, you get streaming responses, token usage callbacks, and chunked inputs for RAG patterns. LlamaIndex support is similar — we provide a wrapper so LlamaIndex can call Redwood directly with embedding endpoints and text-generation. There are a few example notebooks in our repo.
[01:32] Elena Park: Any known issues with LlamaIndex or LangChain versions? We have a slightly older LangChain in prod.
[01:36] Marcus O'Neill: We usually recommend LangChain >= 0.1x (note: version numbers vary), older versions may require a small shim; we can provide a compatibility snippet. Transcription note: I said zero point one x, but I meant the 1.x line earlier, apologies for the confusion.
[01:47] Ravi Singh: Good to know. For our prod traffic, we need a gateway in front of Redwood so we can implement feature flags and route based on cost — is using a proxy supported?
[01:54] Grace Li: Absolutely. We commonly see two patterns: 1) a lightweight API gateway/proxy in your VPC that does auth, rate limiting and routing to either Hosted or Dedicated backends; or 2) direct SDK calls from services with a sidecar that handles retries and batching. Both are supported. For hosted customers we provide a stable public endpoint and API keys; for dedicated/private you get private endpoints in your network.
[02:12] Marta Lopez: If we route through a central gateway, can we still get per-route observability?
[02:15] Marcus O'Neill: Yes, as long as you pass route metadata (we support headers like x-redwood-route or x-rd-route) we surface metrics. If you perform aggregation in the gateway, that can obscure some low-level traces; we recommend passing through request-level metadata so the control plane can join traces.
[02:30] Elena Park: About rate limits, what's the difference between rate limiting at the API key level vs route level? We want to prevent a runaway job from consuming all tokens.
[02:37] Marcus O'Neill: We have per-key and per-route quotas. You can define quotas per API key and also attach quotas to routes or model names. There's burst capacity settings for Dedicated where you can allow short bursts above committed throughput. Hosted has soft burst for small spikes, Dedicated has configurable autoscaling policies and guaranteed throughput.
[02:51] Ravi Singh: Is quota enforcement done at the gateway or at Redwood's edge? If we run private, we want enforcement inside our network.
[02:58] Grace Li: For Hosted and Dedicated, enforcement is on Redwood's control plane/edge. For Private (VPC/on-prem) you can choose to enforce quotas locally — our private control plane can run on your network so enforcement happens there. There is also an enterprise mode where you deploy a policy engine alongside the private control plane.
[03:12] Elena Park: Switching to embeddings — we plan to use embeddings for search (near real-time). Can we control embedding model versions and pin them?
[03:18] Marcus O'Neill: Yes. Our model catalog lets you pin model versions; for Dedicated/Private you can also pin quantization profiles. For hosted we manage model updates but we expose a model version param so you can opt into upgrades.
[03:29] Marta Lopez: How about KV cache and prefix caching? We saw notes about KV cache in the docs but unclear how it interacts with multitenant hosted environment.
[03:36] Marcus O'Neill: The KV cache is per-session and helps with chat latency — we maintain per-connection KV caches and for hosted customers we use namespaced caches to avoid cross-tenant leakage. For Dedicated/Private you have more control — you can colocate cache with your deployment. There may be slight differences in cache eviction policy depending on deployment.
[03:52] Elena Park: Understood. Any limit on sequence length or MATH constraints? We expect a lot of long-context documents.
[03:57] Marcus O'Neill: Sequence length depends on the model you pick; some of our curated models support 32k tokens, others are 8k. We can recommend models based on your profile. There's also tokenization differences to consider — our Optimize toolkit can suggest quant and model pairings for cost tradeoffs.
[04:12] Ravi Singh: On cost modeling — can you share a simple per-1000-token cost comparison between hosted and dedicated? We want to baseline.
[04:18] Grace Li: We'll send the pricing deck and a cost-model spreadsheet. As a ballpark: Hosted has per-token billing; Dedicated moves to a reserved-capacity model where unit costs decrease with commit size, plus infra fees. Private is licensed with a platform fee + support. We'll follow up with concrete numbers for your traffic.
[04:32] Marta Lopez: Security: our SOC2 and SSO are non-negotiable. Do you support SAML SSO and audit logs for user activity?
[04:38] Marcus O'Neill: Yes, Hosted and Dedicated support SAML/SSO and RBAC. Audit logs are available; for Private you can keep logs on-prem and we support configurable retention policies. We can share our SOC2 report excerpt.
[04:49] Elena Park: Any limitations in the SDK for streaming responses? We use streaming heavily for user-facing chat UI.
[04:53] Marcus O'Neill: Streaming is supported in both SDKs (Python & Node). For high-concurrency streaming we recommend Dedicated or Private to guarantee low tail latency. On Hosted, streaming is optimized but shared infra can have slightly higher tail latency under heavy load.
[05:06] Ravi Singh: About integration with our observability stack (we use Datadog) — do you provide OpenTelemetry spans or a push integration?
[05:12] Marcus O'Neill: We emit trace events and can forward spans to your tracing backend; we have an OpenTelemetry-compatible exporter. For Hosted we can push aggregated metrics and traces to Datadog via API keys; for Private you can forward directly.
[05:24] Marta Lopez: Great. For the LangChain connector, are there examples for RAG at scale? We're concerned about chunk size and embedding costs.
[05:30] Marcus O'Neill: Yes, our repo has RAG examples with recommended chunk sizes and dynamic batching to reduce embedding calls. We also support async batch embedding endpoints which help with throughput.
[05:40] Elena Park: What's the recommended approach for a staged rollout? Start hosted, then Dedicated, then Private?
[05:44] Grace Li: Many customers prototype on Hosted to validate quality and latency, then move to Dedicated for predictable throughput and cost, and finally Private for strict compliance or data residency. But you can also go Dedicated-first if you need strict isolation. The API and SDK are the same so code changes are minimal.
[05:59] Ravi Singh: Can you do canary rollouts or A/B tests across model versions?
[06:02] Marcus O'Neill: Yes, rollouts are first-class in the Console — canary deploys, A/B tests, automatic fallback policies. You can route traffic by percentage to different model versions or model variants.
[06:12] Elena Park: About the gateway/proxy again — if we implement our own rate-limiter at the gateway, is there a recommended header to pass the original request id for tracing?
[06:18] Marcus O'Neill: Use x-request-id and x-rd-route for route metadata; passing those helps join traces in the Console.
[06:24] [00:06:24] Marta Lopez: (laughs) I keep forgetting headers.
[06:27] [00:06:27] Grace Li: No worries. Ok, anything else we should cover?
[06:30] Elena Park: Billing: do you support multiple API keys per account for different product teams?
[06:33] Grace Li: Yes. Per-team API keys with separate quotas are typical. You can also set per-key billing codes for chargeback.
[06:39] Ravi Singh: For Dedicated, what's the typical lead time to provision GPU pools?
[06:42] Marcus O'Neill: Typical provisioning is 4-8 weeks depending on region and configuration; if you need faster, we have some pre-warmed options or can use hosted temporarily.
[06:50] Marta Lopez: For Private on-prem, what's involved in the on-prem package? We are partly on GCP and partly on our own data centers.
[06:56] Marcus O'Neill: The on-prem package includes a private control plane, deployment manifests for Kubernetes, connectors for KMS, and a data plane that runs inference workers. We do a short on-site or remote kickoff for networking and integration with your KMS/SIAM. The package supports hybrid cloud too.
[07:09] Elena Park: Any gotchas with model quantization when running on our infra?
[07:13] Marcus O'Neill: Quantization can reduce memory and cost, but there's a small quality delta on some tasks. Our Optimize toolkit will recommend quant profiles per workload and run evals to detect regressions.
[07:23] Ravi Singh: Can we get an evaluation harness to run our prompts and metric targets?
[07:26] Grace Li: Yes, we have an evals harness that runs prompt sets, compares outputs across models, and reports regressions. We'll include that in the follow-up.
[07:33] Elena Park: On the networking side, if we use VPC peering for Dedicated, do you require any special CIDR ranges or NAT gateways?
[07:40] Marcus O'Neill: There are networking requirements; we'll share a VPC checklist — generally you need egress rules, specific port ranges for the control plane, and support for peering or private link depending on cloud. We'll include the checklist with the follow-up.
[07:53] Grace Li: Quick recap before we close: we'll send pricing + cost model, SOC2 excerpt and private deployment checklist, short benchmark/evangel plan from Marcus, and we'd like the Novus team to send traffic profile and sequence length distribution. Any objections?
[08:05] Marta Lopez: Sounds good.
[08:07] Ravi Singh: No objections. We'll aim to get the traffic profile by Monday.
[08:11] Elena Park: Schedule the technical deep-dive for 1/20 please.
[08:14] Grace Li: Will do. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[08:18] Marta Lopez: Thanks Grace, Marcus. Bye.

End of transcript.
